To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the use of health care services is strongly related to multimorbidity, and 2) the prevalence and incidence of multimorbidity are increasing.
multimorbidity is associated with higher health expenditures and that a simple count of the number of chronic conditions does not capture the complexity of multimorbidity.
the number of comorbidities is a better predictor than the presence of any single disease, and that the most common comorbidity groups are those with 3 or more comorbidities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model that will enable us to predict the future healthcare expenditure of the UK population by age, sex and disease category.
how multimorbidity affects the healthcare costs and utilization of individuals with chronic conditions, and whether there are differences in the effects across the different conditions.
the development of a method for predicting future health expenditure by age, sex and multimorbidity groups, based on current expenditure and the expected change in prevalence of multimorbidity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong relationship between multimorbidity and healthcare expenditure.

the most effective method for predicting future healthcare expenditure would be to group individuals into multimorbidity groups based on their comorbidities and then use the mean healthcare expenditure of the group as an estimate of the individuals healthcare expenditure in the future.
the use of health care resources by multimorbid patients can be predicted by the number of diseases and by the number and the type of the diseases in the multimorbidity group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the data presented in this paper show that the prevalence of multimorbidity is higher among older adults in the UK, and that the prevalence increases with increasing age and is more common among women.
the results indicate that the most important factors in the prediction of future healthcare expenditure are multimorbidity and age.
we have shown that the prevalence of chronic conditions in a population is not the only determinant of healthcare costs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the 2016 ICD-10-CM codes to identify chronic conditions is a reasonable alternative to using the 1999 ICD-9-CM codes.
we need to think about how we are measuring multimorbidity and how this is being used to predict healthcare resource utilization.
the use of a simple measure such as the number of chronic conditions can be misleading in terms of predicting healthcare expenditure.
